databases-q2.testing: that you reach for a window function, know why the filter goes outside, and can say what happens with ties.
databases-q2.trap: filtering on the window function in the same WHERE, or a GROUP BY with MAX that can only ever return one row per group.
databases-q2.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Read the tables "One table, employees, with a department id and a salary. The output is up to two rows per department: the department, the name and the salary."
2 · Name the pattern "This is top-N per group. The move is to number the rows inside each department, ordered by salary, and then keep the first two."
3 · Write it "So I use ROW_NUMBER with PARTITION BY department and ORDER BY salary descending, in a subquery, and filter on the row number in the outer query."
4 · Trace it on data "On the sample, Engineering has salaries three hundred, two-sixty, two-fifty and two-fifty. The numbering gives one, two, three, four, so I keep Asha and Dev."
5 · Variants and traps "The follow-up is always ties. ROW_NUMBER gives exactly two rows and picks arbitrarily between equal salaries, so I add a tie-breaker. DENSE_RANK gives the top two salary levels and keeps everyone on them. I'd ask which they want."
6 · How it performs "For performance, an index on department and salary lets the engine read each partition already sorted. On a very large table with few departments, a lateral join that fetches two rows per department can be cheaper."
Close "Partition, order, number, then filter outside."

stages.name: Read the tables
stages.claim: one table, N rows per group out
stages.html:
"I say what one output row is before writing anything."

employees(id, name, dept_id, manager_id, salary, hired_on)
id name dept_id salary
1 Asha 1 300
2 Bo 1 250
3 Chen 1 250
4 Dev 1 260
5 Eli 2 200
6 Fay 2 220
7 Gus 2 150

Output: dept_id, name, salary, at most two rows per department.

stages.name: Name the pattern
stages.html:
"'Per department' plus 'top two' means rank inside a partition."

Pattern:partition by the grouporder by the measurenumber the rowsfilter on the number, outside
Clue in the question Points to
"in each…", "per…" PARTITION BY
"top", "highest", "latest" ORDER BY … DESC inside the window
"two", "N" a filter on the row number

A plain GROUP BY dept_id with MAX(salary) returns one row per group and loses the name, so it can't answer this.

stages.name: Write it
stages.claim: number in a subquery, filter outside
stages.html:
"The window function runs after WHERE, so its result has to be filtered one level up." Run on SQLite 3.51.

SELECT dept_id, name, salary FROM (
  SELECT e.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC, id) AS rn
  FROM employees e
) WHERE rn <= 2;
dept_id name salary
1 Asha 300
1 Dev 260
2 Fay 220
2 Eli 200

stages.name: Trace it on data
stages.html:
"Department 1, with all three ranking functions side by side." Run on the sample.

name salary ROW_NUMBER RANK DENSE_RANK
Asha 300 1 1 1
Dev 260 2 2 2
Bo 250 3 3 3
Chen 250 4 3 3

rn <= 2 keeps the two bold rows. Bo and Chen tie on 250: ROW_NUMBER separates them (by id, because I asked it to), while RANK and DENSE_RANK give both a 3.

stages.name: Variants and traps
stages.claim: ties, and where the filter goes
stages.html:
"Which function I use is a question about ties."

They want Use On a tie at the cut-off
Exactly N rows per group ROW_NUMBER + a tie-breaker one is picked, deterministically
Everyone on the top N salary levels DENSE_RANK all tied rows kept
Top N, with gaps after ties RANK can return more or fewer than N
Trap What happens
WHERE ROW_NUMBER() … <= 2 in the same query an error: window functions aren't allowed in WHERE
No tie-breaker in ORDER BY different rows on different runs
GROUP BY + MAX one row per group, and no way to get the second

Dialect: PostgreSQL has no QUALIFY; some warehouses do (QUALIFY rn <= 2), which removes the subquery.

stages.name: How it performs
stages.claim: an index that matches the window
stages.html:
"The window needs each partition sorted; an index can hand it over already sorted."

Design Effect
Index on (dept_id, salary DESC) each partition is read in order; no sort
No index a full scan and a sort of the whole table
Few groups, huge table a lateral join (one indexed lookup of N rows per group) reads far fewer rows

What breaks at scale: the window numbers every row before the filter discards most of them. With a hundred million rows and ten departments, that's a hundred million rows numbered to return twenty.

Fix layer: the query for correctness, the index for cost.

followUps.question: "Why not just put the row number in the WHERE clause?"
followUps.html:
Because WHERE runs before window functions are computed.

Logical order:FROMWHEREGROUP BYHAVINGwindow functionsSELECTORDER BY

So the number doesn't exist yet when WHERE runs.

followUps.question: 🧪 On the sample, what does  return for department 1?
followUps.html:
All four employees.

salary levels: 300 (1), 260 (2), 250 (3)
Bo and Chen both sit on level 3 → 4 rows for "top 3"

That's the difference to state out loud: N levels, not N rows.

followUps.question: How would you do it without window functions?
followUps.html:
With a correlated count: keep a row if fewer than two salaries in its department are higher.

Approach Cost
Correlated subquery counting higher salaries one subquery per row; slow on large groups
Window function one pass per partition

followUps.question: A department has only one employee. What comes back?
followUps.html:
One row for that department.

  • "Up to N" is what the query gives.
  • If they want exactly N rows padded with NULLs, that needs a generated series joined in.

followUps.question: This runs on a 500-million-row table every minute. What do you change?
followUps.html:
Stop computing it from scratch.

Option Trade
An index matching the partition and order cheaper reads; more write cost
A lateral join per department reads N rows per group
A materialised or incrementally maintained result fast reads; staleness to state

dontSay: "I'd group by department and take the max." — that returns one row and no name.
"Row number and rank are the same." — they differ exactly on ties.
"I'd filter on the row number in the WHERE." — it isn't computed yet.
"It works on my data." — say what happens on a tie.

databases-q6.testing: that you know an anti-join, and that you know why NOT IN silently returns nothing when the subquery contains a NULL.
databases-q6.trap: WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders) on a nullable column.
databases-q6.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Read the tables "Two tables: customers, and orders with a customer id that can be NULL. I want one row per customer who has no matching order."
2 · Name the pattern "This is an anti-join: rows on the left with no match on the right."
3 · Write it "I'd write it with NOT EXISTS and a correlated subquery. It reads as the question does, and it's safe with NULLs."
4 · Trace it on data "On the sample, Acme and Birla have orders and Corex doesn't, so it returns Corex."
5 · Variants and traps "The trap is NOT IN. One order in the sample has a NULL customer id, and with that NULL in the list the NOT IN version returns zero rows. Any comparison with NULL is unknown, so 'not in' can never be true. The LEFT JOIN with IS NULL form is also correct."
6 · How it performs "With an index on orders customer id, the engine runs it as an anti-join and stops at the first match per customer. All three correct forms usually get the same plan."
Close "NOT EXISTS for 'has none', and I always check whether the subquery column can be NULL."

stages.name: Read the tables
stages.html:
"The NULL in customer_id is the detail that decides the answer."

customers(id, name)
orders(id, customer_id, amount, status, created_at)   -- customer_id can be NULL
customers.id name orders.id customer_id
1 Acme 1, 2, 4, 7 1
2 Birla 3, 5 2
3 Corex 6 NULL

Output: the customers with no order. Here, Corex.

stages.name: Name the pattern
stages.html:
"'Never', 'no', 'without' in the question means rows with no match."

Pattern:for each left rowdoes any right row match?keep it
Clue in the question Pattern
"who have never…", "with no…", "missing" anti-join
"who have at least one…" semi-join (EXISTS)

stages.name: Write it
stages.html:
"It reads like the question, and NULLs can't break it." Run on SQLite 3.51.

SELECT c.name FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);
name
Corex

SELECT 1 because only existence matters; no columns are read from the subquery.

stages.name: Trace it on data
stages.claim: three forms on the same rows
stages.html:
"Same tables, three queries, and one of them is wrong." All run on the sample.

Form Result
NOT EXISTS (… o.customer_id = c.id) Corex
LEFT JOIN orders o ON … WHERE o.id IS NULL Corex
c.id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders) no rows
NOT IN (… WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL) Corex

Why the third is empty, for Corex (id = 3):

3 NOT IN (1, 1, 2, 1, 2, NULL, 1)
= 3 <> 1 AND 3 <> 2 AND 3 <> NULL
= TRUE   AND TRUE   AND UNKNOWN     ← a comparison with NULL is unknown
= UNKNOWN                            ← WHERE keeps only TRUE, so the row is dropped

stages.name: Variants and traps
stages.html:
"The forms differ in what NULLs and duplicate matches do."

Form NULL in the subquery Duplicates on the right
NOT EXISTS safe irrelevant
LEFT JOIN … IS NULL safe irrelevant for the anti-join
NOT IN returns nothing irrelevant
EXCEPT (ids only) NULLs compare as equal removed
Variant asked next Change
"…in the last 90 days" the date filter goes inside the subquery, not in the outer WHERE
"…who never paid" AND o.status = 'paid' inside the subquery
LEFT JOIN form test IS NULL on a column that's never NULL in a real match, like the primary key

stages.name: How it performs
stages.html:
"With an index on the join column, the engine stops at the first match."

Design Effect
Index on orders(customer_id) one probe per customer; stop at the first hit
No index the planner hashes orders once, or scans it per customer
NOT IN on a nullable column the planner often can't use an anti-join at all

What breaks at scale: a customers table of millions against an orders table of billions is fine with the index. Without it, it's a hash of the whole orders table.

Fix layer: the query; and the schema: a NOT NULL constraint on the foreign key removes the trap at the source.

followUps.question: "NOT IN is simpler and gives the same result."
followUps.html:
Only until one NULL appears in the list.

NOT IN NOT EXISTS
No NULLs in the subquery correct correct
One NULL zero rows, no error correct

It fails silently, which is the worst way to fail.

followUps.question: 🧪 The order with the NULL customer id is deleted. What does the NOT IN version return now?
followUps.html:
Corex.

3 NOT IN (1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1) = TRUE     ← no NULL left in the list

So the query "works" until the next NULL arrives, which is why it passes tests and fails in production.

followUps.question: Why does the LEFT JOIN form test ?
followUps.html:
Because the primary key is never NULL in a real match.

  • Matched row: o.id has a value.
  • No match: the join fills every o column with NULL.
  • Testing a nullable column would confuse "no match" with "matched a NULL".

followUps.question: How do you count orders per customer, including customers with none?
followUps.html:
LEFT JOIN and count a column from the right side.

Expression Customers with no orders
COUNT(o.id) 0
COUNT(*) 1 : it counts the NULL-filled row

followUps.question: How would you stop the NULL from being possible?
followUps.html:
With constraints, so the query can't be surprised.

Constraint Effect
customer_id NOT NULL no orphan orders
A foreign key to customers(id) no orders for customers that don't exist

If a guest order is a real case, it gets its own explicit representation, not a NULL.

dontSay: "NOT IN and NOT EXISTS are the same." — not when a NULL is present.
"I'd use a LEFT JOIN and check for NULL." — say on which column, and why that one.
"It returned no rows, so everyone has ordered." — check the subquery for NULLs first.
"NULL means zero or empty." — it means unknown.

databases-q8.testing: whether you know the gaps-and-islands trick, and can explain why subtracting a row number from a date gives a constant inside a streak.
databases-q8.trap: a self-join on "yesterday", or forgetting to remove duplicate days first.
databases-q8.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Read the tables "One table, logins, with a user id and a login date. A user can log in more than once a day. I want one row per user with their longest run of consecutive days."
2 · Name the pattern "This is gaps and islands. A streak is an island of consecutive dates, and I need a label that's the same for every row in one island."
3 · Write it "The trick: number each user's distinct days in date order, and subtract that number from the date. Inside a streak both go up by one each day, so the difference stays constant. Then I group by that difference, count, and take the maximum."
4 · Trace it on data "User one logs in on the first, second and third, then the seventh and eighth. Date minus row number gives the twenty-eighth of February three times, then the third of March twice. Two islands, sizes three and two, so the answer is three."
5 · Variants and traps "The trap is duplicates. Two logins on one day give two row numbers for one date and break the arithmetic, so I take distinct days first."
6 · How it performs "It's one sort per user. An index on user id and login date makes that an ordered read."
Close "Date minus row number is the island id."

stages.name: Read the tables
stages.html:
"The unit is a day, and the table may hold more than one row per day."

logins(user_id, login_date)
user_id login_date
1 2026-03-01, 03-02, 03-03, 03-07, 03-08
2 2026-03-01, 03-03, 03-08

Output: user_id, longest_streak. Expected: user 1 → 3, user 2 → 1.

stages.name: Name the pattern
stages.html:
"I need a value that's identical within a streak and different between streaks."

Pattern:dedupe daysrow number per user by datedate − row number = island idcount per islandmax per user
Clue in the question Pattern
"consecutive", "streak", "in a row" gaps and islands
"uninterrupted period", "runs of the same status" the same

Why it works: inside a streak the date rises by one day per row and so does the row number, so their difference doesn't move. A gap makes the date jump while the row number rises by one, so the difference changes.

stages.name: Write it
stages.claim: subtract the row number from the date
stages.html:
"Three steps as three CTE levels." Run on SQLite 3.51.

WITH d AS (SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_date FROM logins),
g AS (
  SELECT user_id, login_date,
         julianday(login_date) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS grp
  FROM d
)
SELECT user_id, MAX(n) AS longest_streak FROM (
  SELECT user_id, grp, COUNT(*) AS n FROM g
  GROUP BY user_id, grp
) GROUP BY user_id;
user_id longest_streak
1 3
2 1

stages.name: Trace it on data
stages.html:
"User 1, with the intermediate columns the query computes." Run on the sample; the last column is date minus row number, shown as a date.

login_date row number date − row number island
03-01 1 02-28 A
03-02 2 02-28 A
03-03 3 02-28 A
03-07 4 03-03 B
03-08 5 03-03 B

Island A has 3 rows, island B has 2. MAX over the island sizes gives 3.

The island id itself (28 February) means nothing. It only has to be the same within a streak.

stages.name: Variants and traps
stages.claim: duplicates, and what they ask next
stages.html:
"The first CTE isn't decoration."

Trap What happens
No DISTINCT, two logins on 03-02 row numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 for dates 01, 02, 02, 03 → the island id changes mid-streak
A self-join on date = date + 1 finds pairs, not runs; needs recursion to chain them
Timestamps, not dates truncate to a day first, in the user's time zone
Variant asked next Change
"Current streak, as of today" keep the island whose last date is today or yesterday
"Start and end of each streak" MIN(login_date), MAX(login_date) per island
"Streaks of at least 7 days" HAVING COUNT(*) >= 7 on the island level
PostgreSQL login_date - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (…)::int in place of julianday

stages.name: How it performs
stages.html:
"The cost is the sort that the window needs."

Design Effect
Index on (user_id, login_date) each user's days are read in order; the DISTINCT and the window share it
No index a sort of the whole table
Billions of events pre-aggregate to one row per user per day, then run this on the daily table

What breaks at scale: recomputing every user's history on each request. A streak counter maintained on write, or a daily batch, replaces it.

Fix layer: the query for correctness, a daily rollup for cost.

followUps.question: "Join the table to itself on date = date + 1."
followUps.html:
That finds adjacent pairs, not the length of a run.

Self-join Date − row number
One join per extra day of streak one pass
Needs recursion for runs of unknown length a group-by

followUps.question: 🧪 User 1 also logged in twice on 03-02 and you skip the DISTINCT. What's the longest streak the query reports?
followUps.html:
2, not 3.

dates:        03-01  03-02  03-02  03-03  03-07  03-08
row number:     1      2      3      4      5      6
difference:   02-28  02-28  02-27  02-27  03-02  03-02     ← the streak is split in two
island sizes:    2             2             2

followUps.question: Why does the subtraction give a constant?
followUps.html:
Both sides rise by exactly one per row inside a streak.

date:        d,   d+1, d+2      ← consecutive days
row number:  r,   r+1, r+2
difference:  d−r, d−r, d−r      ← constant

followUps.question: How would you get the current streak only?
followUps.html:
Keep the island that ends today or yesterday.

  • Per island: MAX(login_date) as its end.
  • Filter: end ≥ yesterday.
  • No such island: the current streak is 0.

followUps.question: This powers a "streak" badge shown on every page load. Do you run this query?
followUps.html:
No. I maintain the number on write.

Approach Cost per page load
Run the query a scan of the user's history
A current_streak and last_login_date column, updated on login one row read

The query stays as the audit that rebuilds or checks the counter.

dontSay: "I'd loop over the days in the application." — it's one query.
"I'd self-join on the previous day." — that gives pairs, not run lengths.
"The grouping column is the streak's start date." — it's an arbitrary constant.
"Duplicates don't matter." — they split the island.

databases-q19.testing: the leftmost-prefix rule, the equality-then-range ordering, and that you'd confirm with a plan.
databases-q19.trap: ordering the columns by "most selective first", whatever the queries look like.
databases-q19.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "A composite index is one B-tree sorted by the first column, then by the second within each value of the first. It's like a phone book sorted by surname, then first name."
2 · Mechanism "So a query can use it from the left. Customer id alone: a seek. Customer id and a range on created-at: a seek on both. Created-at alone: the index can't be entered, because dates are only sorted within each customer."
3 · Where it breaks "It breaks in three ways: the leading column is missing from the predicate, a function wraps the column, or a range on an earlier column stops later columns from being used for seeking."
4 · How I'd use it "The rule I design by is equality columns first, then one range column, then columns for sorting. And I check the plan, because that's the only proof the index is used."
5 · Adjacent concept "If the index also holds every column the query selects, the table isn't read at all. That's a covering index."
Close "Usable from the left; equality first, then the range; and the plan decides."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html:
"The index is one sorted list of pairs."

customer_id created_at → row
1 2026-01-05 order 1
1 2026-01-20 order 2
1 2026-02-14 order 4
1 2026-03-15 order 7
2 2026-02-03 order 3
2 2026-03-01 order 5

Within customer 1 the dates are in order. Across the whole index they are not: 2026-02-03 comes after 2026-03-15.

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
"What each predicate gets from the index." Plans produced by SQLite 3.51 on the sample, with the index on (customer_id, created_at).

Query predicate Plan line Verdict
customer_id = 1 AND created_at > … SEARCH … USING INDEX (customer_id=? AND created_at>?) seek on both
customer_id = 1 SEARCH … USING INDEX (customer_id=?) seek on the prefix
created_at > … SCAN orders full scan
SELECT customer_id, created_at … WHERE customer_id = 1 SEARCH … USING COVERING INDEX (customer_id=?) index only
substr(created_at,1,7) = '2026-02' SCAN orders function on the column
Seek path:find the first entry for customer 1within it, find the first date after the boundread forward until the customer changes

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.html:
"Three ways a correct-looking index goes unused."

Break Why Fix
The leading column isn't in the WHERE the second column isn't sorted globally a second index, or a different column order
A function or cast on the column the index stores the raw value rewrite as a range, or an expression index
A range on the first column, equality on the second after the range, the index is only useful as a filter put the equality column first
Low selectivity reading most of the table through an index is slower than a scan let it scan

stages.name: How I'd use it
stages.html:
"I order the columns from the query, and prove it with the plan."

Rule:equality columnsone range columnsort columnsincluded columns for covering
query: WHERE customer_id = 1 AND created_at > '2026-02-01' ORDER BY created_at

no index:                SCAN orders
                         USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY          ← scan, then sort
index (created_at):      SEARCH … USING INDEX (created_at>?)   ← seeks on the date only
index (customer_id,
       created_at):      SEARCH … USING INDEX (customer_id=? AND created_at>?)
                                                               ← seeks on both; already in order, no sort

All three plans were produced on the sample. The third also removes the sort, because the index returns rows already ordered by date within the customer.

Measure before adding: every index is paid for on every insert, update and delete.

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html:
"If the index has every column the query needs, the table is never touched."

Ordinary index Covering index
Reads index, then the row index only
Plan says index scan index-only scan (PostgreSQL) / USING COVERING INDEX (SQLite)
Cost — a wider index: more write work and memory
PostgreSQL — INCLUDE (col) adds payload without widening the key

SELECT * defeats it: the query now needs columns the index doesn't hold.

followUps.question: "Put the most selective column first."
followUps.html:
Order by how the queries filter, not by selectivity alone.

Query Best order
a = ? AND b > ? (a, b), even if b is more selective
a = ? AND b = ? either; pick the one other queries also lead with

A range in the first position stops the second column from seeking.

followUps.question: 🧪 With an index on , can  across all customers avoid a sort?
followUps.html:
No.

index order: (1, Jan) (1, Feb) (1, Mar) (2, Feb) (2, Mar) …
needed:      Jan, Feb, Feb, Mar, Mar …        ← dates are ordered only within a customer

That query wants an index that leads with created_at.

followUps.question: Do I need a separate index on  as well?
followUps.html:
No. The composite index already serves it.

  • (customer_id, created_at) covers every query that leads with customer_id.
  • A separate (customer_id) index is redundant write cost.

followUps.question: How do you know the index is actually used in production?
followUps.html:
From the plan and from usage statistics.

Evidence Tells you
EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the real query which index, and actual rows
Index usage counters indexes that are never scanned: candidates to drop

followUps.question: A table has fourteen indexes. What's your concern?
followUps.html:
Write cost and overlap.

Problem Check
Every write maintains all fourteen insert and update latency
Prefix duplicates (a) next to (a, b)
Never used zero scans in the usage counters

dontSay: "The index has that column, so the query uses it." — only from the left.
"Most selective column first." — equality before range, by the queries.
"I added an index and it's faster." — show the plan.
"More indexes can't hurt." — every write pays for each one.

databases-q22.testing: that you can name the anomalies, know the defaults differ by engine, and know the application must retry at the strict levels.
databases-q22.trap: assuming "repeatable read" means the same thing on every engine, or that the default level prevents lost updates.
databases-q22.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "An isolation level says which effects of other running transactions mine is allowed to see. Each level is defined by the anomalies it still permits."
2 · Mechanism "There are four standard levels. Read uncommitted allows dirty reads. Read committed stops those and still allows non-repeatable reads and phantoms. Repeatable read gives me a stable view of rows I've read; the standard still allows phantoms. Serializable allows none: the result must match some one-at-a-time order."
3 · Where it breaks "Two things catch people. Defaults differ: PostgreSQL defaults to read committed, MySQL's InnoDB to repeatable read. And PostgreSQL's repeatable read is snapshot isolation, which has no phantoms and still allows write skew."
4 · How I'd use it "I stay on the default and protect each invariant explicitly: an atomic update, a row lock, or a version column. For an invariant that spans several rows, I use serializable for that transaction, and the application retries when it's told to."
5 · Adjacent concept "Underneath, most engines implement this with multi-version concurrency control, so readers and writers don't block each other."
Close "Name the anomaly, pick the lowest level or lock that prevents it, and retry on failure."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.claim: levels are defined by what they allow
stages.html:
"Four anomalies, in plain words."

Anomaly What happens
Dirty read I read a change another transaction hasn't committed, and it rolls back
Non-repeatable read I read a row twice and get two different values
Phantom I run the same range query twice and get a different set of rows
Lost update two transactions read, modify and write; one overwrites the other
Write skew two transactions each read a set, each write a different row, and together break a rule

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
"The SQL standard's table, plus the two anomalies it doesn't list."

Level Dirty read Non-repeatable read Phantom Lost update Write skew
Read uncommitted possible possible possible possible possible
Read committed — possible possible possible possible
Repeatable read (standard) — — possible engine-dependent possible
Serializable — — — — —
Engine Default Note
PostgreSQL read committed its repeatable read is snapshot isolation: no phantoms; a concurrent update of the same row fails and must be retried
MySQL InnoDB repeatable read uses gap locks to block many phantoms

Engine behaviour as generally documented; I'd confirm against the version in use.

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.html:
"A lost update at read committed, as two sessions." PostgreSQL-style read committed.

Time Session A Session B
1 SELECT stock → 5
2 SELECT stock → 5
3 UPDATE … SET stock = 4 (5 − 1)
4 commit
5 UPDATE … SET stock = 4 (5 − 1)
6 commit
Result: stock = 4, two items sold

Write skew at snapshot isolation. Rule: at least one doctor on call.

Time Session A (Alice) Session B (Bob)
1 count on call → 2 count on call → 2
2 "2 > 1, I can leave": sets Alice off call "2 > 1, I can leave": sets Bob off call
3 commit commit
Result: nobody on call

Neither wrote a row the other wrote, so a snapshot sees no conflict. Only serializable catches it.

stages.name: How I'd use it
stages.claim: protect the invariant, not the whole workload
stages.html:
"I pick the smallest tool that prevents the specific anomaly."

Invariant Tool
A counter or balance on one row an atomic statement: UPDATE … SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0
Read, decide, then write one row SELECT … FOR UPDATE, or a version column with a check
A rule across several rows (on call, no overlapping bookings) serializable for that transaction, or a constraint that encodes the rule
A report that must be self-consistent repeatable read / a snapshot
At serializable:runcommitretry the whole transactioncommit

The retry is the application's job. A strict level without a retry loop turns anomalies into errors that reach users.

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html:
"Isolation levels are the contract; MVCC is how most engines keep it."

Lock-based MVCC
Readers and writers block each other don't block each other
A reader sees the current row, when it can get a lock a snapshot of committed versions
Cost waiting dead row versions to clean up

What each level means in practice is "which snapshot do I read from, and when is it taken": per statement at read committed, per transaction at repeatable read.

Fix layer: the transaction design in the application, backed by constraints in the database.

followUps.question: "We use transactions, so concurrent updates are safe."
followUps.html:
A transaction gives atomicity. Isolation is a separate setting, and the default allows lost updates.

Belief Reality at read committed
"Read then write in a transaction is safe" two transactions can both read 5 and both write 4
"The database will detect it" not at that level

followUps.question: 🧪 In the stock example, both sessions run  with no SELECT first. Result?
followUps.html:
3. No update is lost.

A: stock = stock − 1  → 4, commit
B: waits for A's row lock, re-reads the committed value 4, → 3

The read and the write are one statement, so there's no gap for another transaction to slip into.

followUps.question: Why not run everything at serializable?
followUps.html:
It costs throughput and requires retries everywhere.

  • More aborts under contention.
  • Every transaction needs a retry loop.
  • Most work doesn't have a cross-row invariant to protect.

followUps.question: What's the difference between a non-repeatable read and a phantom?
followUps.html:
One is about a row changing; the other about the set of rows changing.

Non-repeatable read Phantom
Second read differs because an existing row was updated a row was inserted or deleted in the range
Stopped by repeatable read serializable (or snapshot / gap locks, by engine)

followUps.question: How do you find isolation bugs before production?
followUps.html:
By testing the invariant under concurrency, not the code path alone.

Technique Finds
Concurrent tests that run the same operation in parallel and assert the invariant lost updates, write skew
A constraint that encodes the rule violations become errors, whatever the code does
Serialisation-failure and deadlock rates in monitoring contention that needs redesign

dontSay: "Repeatable read prevents phantoms." — by the standard it doesn't; by engine it varies.
"The default level is safe." — it allows lost updates.
"Serializable everywhere." — with what retry logic?
"ACID means no anomalies." — isolation has levels.

databases-q30.testing: that you start from access patterns and consistency needs, and can say what each choice gives up.
databases-q30.trap: "NoSQL because it scales", with no queries written down.
databases-q30.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "The axis is query flexibility against predictable scale. A relational database lets me ask questions I haven't thought of yet. A NoSQL store makes a few known questions fast at any size, and makes the others hard."
2 · Where relational wins "Relational wins when I need joins, ad-hoc queries, transactions across several rows, and constraints the database enforces. That's most business systems."
3 · Where NoSQL wins "NoSQL wins when the access patterns are few and known in advance, the volume or write rate is beyond one node, or the records vary in shape. Key-value for lookups, document for aggregates read as a whole, wide-column for huge write volume by partition key."
4 · The deciding question "So I write down the queries first. Can I list every access pattern today? Do any need a transaction across records? What's the scale, with a number? If I can't list the patterns, I'm not ready for a store that requires them."
5 · What I'd pick "My default is one relational database until a measured limit says otherwise. Then I add a specialised store for the one workload that needs it, and accept that keeping two stores in sync is now my problem."
Close "Queries first, then consistency, then scale; the product name comes last."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
"Each side buys one thing with the other."

Relational NoSQL (as a family)
Queries any, including ones added later the ones you designed for
Joins in the database in the application, or denormalised away
Transactions across rows and tables usually within one key or partition
Schema enforced flexible; enforced in code
Scale-out harder: replicas, then sharding built in, by partition key
Pick when the questions aren't all known the questions are few, known and huge

stages.name: Where relational wins
stages.html:
"Four needs that a relational engine gives for free."

Need Example
Ad-hoc queries and reporting "orders by region last quarter", asked next month
Multi-row transactions move money between two accounts
Constraints unique email, foreign keys, no overlapping bookings
Many relationships customers, orders, items, invoices, refunds

A single well-run relational node, with replicas, carries more load than most products ever reach.

stages.name: Where NoSQL wins
stages.html:
"Four models, each shaped like one kind of query."

Model Shaped for Example
Key-value lookup by key sessions, caches, feature flags
Document one aggregate read and written whole; varying fields a product catalogue
Wide-column huge write volume; query by partition key and a sorted range time-series events per device
Graph relationships: paths, neighbours, many hops fraud rings, recommendations
Design order flips:relational: entitiesnormalisequeries later
NoSQL:queries firstkeys per queryduplicate data per pattern

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
"A table I fill in before naming a product."

Access pattern Frequency Needs a transaction across records? Consistency needed
Get order by id very high no read-your-writes
Orders for a customer, newest first high no seconds stale is fine
Place order: stock down, order in, payment recorded high yes strong
Revenue by region, ad hoc low no minutes stale is fine
Reading of the table Choice
A cross-record transaction on the hot path relational for that data
Ad-hoc questions exist relational, or a warehouse fed from it
Only two or three key-based patterns, at very high volume a NoSQL store fits
I can't fill the table in relational: it tolerates not knowing

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.claim: relational first, a second store on evidence
stages.html:
"One store by default; a second one for a measured reason."

Path:one relational databaseindexes, replicas, cachinga specialised store for that one workloadsync by CDC
A second store adds Which I then own
Another consistency model what users see while the two disagree
A sync path CDC or dual writes, and their failures
Operations backups, upgrades, on-call for another system

Measure before moving: the plan and the wait events of the slow queries, write rate against the node's limit, data size against what one machine holds.

Fix layer: data model, chosen from the access patterns.

followUps.question: "NoSQL scales and SQL doesn't."
followUps.html:
Both scale; they scale different things.

Claim Reality
"SQL can't scale" replicas scale reads; partitioning and sharding scale writes, at a cost
"NoSQL scales everything" it scales the access patterns you designed keys for

followUps.question: 🧪 A document store holds orders with the customer's address embedded. The customer changes address. What happens to old orders?
followUps.html:
Nothing, and that may be right or wrong.

embedded copy  → old orders keep the old address      ← correct for "shipped to"
reference      → every order shows the new address    ← correct for "current contact"

Denormalising forces that decision per field; a relational join lets me defer it.

followUps.question: Isn't schemaless more flexible?
followUps.html:
The schema still exists; it moved into the application.

  • Schema on write: the database rejects bad data.
  • Schema on read: every reader handles every old shape, forever.

followUps.question: When would you use both?
followUps.html:
When one workload has a shape the main store handles badly.

Main store Added store For
Relational a cache or key-value store hot lookups
Relational a search engine full-text search
Relational a column store analytics

followUps.question: The team wants to start on a NoSQL store "to be ready for scale". Your response?
followUps.html:
Ask for the access patterns and the number.

  • If the patterns are known and the volume is real, agree.
  • If not, start relational and set the measured trigger for moving: write rate, data size, or a specific query that no longer fits.

dontSay: "NoSQL because it scales." — what, by which key?
"SQL is old technology." — it's the default for good reasons.
"We'll figure out the queries later" with a NoSQL store. — that store needs them first.
"Schemaless means no schema work." — the work moves to the code.

databases-q38.testing: that you get the actual plan before touching anything, and can tell a plan change from data growth from waiting.
databases-q38.trap: adding an index before looking at the plan.
databases-q38.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "The code didn't change, so either the plan changed, the data changed, or the query is waiting on something. Those are three different problems."
2 · Rule out the fakes "First I check that it's the query at all: is it running slowly, or queued behind a lock, a saturated disk, or an exhausted connection pool?"
3 · Confirm with evidence "Then I get the actual plan with timings and compare it with the old one. I look at estimated rows against actual rows. A large gap means stale statistics, and that's usually why the planner switched to a worse join or a scan."
4 · Fix by experiment "I fix the cause the plan shows, one change at a time. Refresh statistics. Add or correct an index. Rewrite a predicate that hides a column inside a function. Pinning a plan is a stopgap only."
5 · Validate "I confirm with the plan again and with the latency percentiles, on production-sized data and for the customer that was slow."
6 · Productionise "Then I make it visible next time: slow-query logging with plans, an alert on the percentile, and statistics kept fresh on the tables that skew."
Close "Fixed means the plan is the right one again, and I'd know within minutes if it flipped."

stages.name: Name it
stages.html:
"'Nothing was deployed' rules out code, not change."

What can change with no deploy Example
The plan statistics went stale, or were refreshed, and the planner chose differently
The data the table grew; one customer became a hundred times larger
The environment a lock holder, a noisy neighbour, a cold cache after a restart
The parameters the same query with a different value takes a different path

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.html:
"Four things make a fast query look slow."

Fake Check
Blocked on a lock lock waits; who holds the lock
Waiting for a connection pool wait time against query time
I/O or CPU saturation host metrics; everything is slow, not this query
A cold cache did the database or the host just restart?

Split the time: total 4 s = waiting for a connection + waiting on locks + executing ← only this part is about the plan

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.claim: the actual plan, estimated against actual
stages.html:
"The plan tells me which of the three it is."

Observation in the plan Likely cause Next action
Estimated 10 rows, actual 500,000 stale or missing statistics refresh statistics
A sequential scan where an index scan used to be the planner now thinks the predicate is unselective, or the index is gone or invalid check the index; check statistics
A nested loop over a huge outer side a bad row estimate chose the wrong join fix the estimate; then the join follows
The same plan, more rows at every node data growth an index that matches, partitioning, or archiving
A sort or hash spilling to disk the working set outgrew memory reduce rows earlier; then memory settings
Fast for most values, slow for one skew: one tenant or status dominates a plan or index for the skewed value

stages.name: Fix by experiment
stages.claim: one change, then the plan again
stages.html:
"What the right index does to a plan." Plans produced by SQLite 3.51 on the sample orders table.

query: WHERE customer_id = 1 AND created_at > '2026-02-01' ORDER BY created_at

before:  SCAN orders
         USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY                   ← reads everything, then sorts
after:   SEARCH orders USING INDEX idx_orders_cust_created
                (customer_id=? AND created_at>?)        ← seeks, already ordered
Experiment 1

Refresh statistics

I run the engine's analyse command on the tables in the query.

Why? A wrong row estimate is the most common reason for a plan flip, and this fixes it without changing anything else.

Best suited when estimated and actual rows differ widely.

Experiment 2

An index that matches the predicate

I add or correct an index: equality columns first, then the range column.

Why? The plan shows a scan and a sort that an index would remove.

Best suited when the plan is stable and simply reads too much.

Experiment 3

Rewrite the predicate

I move a function off the indexed column, or replace OR with a union.

Why? A predicate the index can't seek on forces a scan however good the index is.

Best suited when an index exists and isn't used.

stages.name: Validate
stages.html:
"Faster on my laptop proves nothing."

Check Before After
Plan for the slow value measure measure
p50 / p95 / p99 latency measure measure
Rows read per execution measure measure
Write latency on the table (if an index was added) measure measure

Validated on production-sized data and with the parameter value that was slow, because skew doesn't show on averages.

stages.name: Productionise
stages.html:
"I want the plan captured at the moment it goes wrong."

Practice Detail
Slow-query log with plans the evidence exists when the alert fires
Alert on p95 and p99 per query group minutes, not a customer report
Statistics on skewed, fast-growing tables refreshed more often than the default
Query review for new indexes each one is weighed against its write cost
Plan pinning a time-boxed stopgap with an owner

Fix layer: statistics and indexes in the database; query shape in the application.

followUps.question: "Just add an index on the columns in the WHERE clause."
followUps.html:
Without the plan, that's a guess with a permanent write cost.

Wrong order:slowadd an indexstill slow, or slow again next month
Right order:slowactual planestimates against actualsthe causeone fix

followUps.question: 🧪 The plan says "estimated rows 12, actual rows 480,000". What do you do first?
followUps.html:
Refresh statistics and look at the plan again.

estimate / actual = 12 / 480,000     ← off by a factor of 40,000
a planner that expects 12 rows picks a nested loop; for 480,000 it should hash or scan

If the estimate is still wrong afterwards, the columns are correlated and need extended statistics or a different predicate.

followUps.question: It's slow only for one large customer. Why?
followUps.html:
Skew: the plan that suits a typical customer is wrong for the huge one.

Typical customer Giant customer
An index lookup returns 50 rows the same lookup returns 5 million
Fine a scan or a different index would be better

followUps.question: How do you tell waiting from working?
followUps.html:
From wait events and from the plan's own timings.

  • Execution time in the plan is small, total time is large: it was waiting.
  • Lock-wait and pool-wait metrics say on what.

followUps.question: How do you stop plan flips from being incidents?
followUps.html:
Make them visible and make the hot queries robust.

Guard Effect
Plan capture on slow queries diagnosis in minutes
Indexes that make the good plan obviously cheapest less room for the planner to switch
Load tests on production-sized, skewed data flips found before release

dontSay: "I'd add an index." — after reading the plan.
"Nothing changed, so it must be the database." — data and statistics changed.
"I'd increase the instance size." — that hides a bad plan for a while.
"It's fast when I run it." — with which parameter, on which data?

databases-q40.testing: that you know which statements lock the table and for how long, and that you split the change into steps that can each be rolled back.
databases-q40.trap: one ALTER TABLE … NOT NULL DEFAULT … plus one UPDATE of every row.
databases-q40.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "First I ask which engine and version, because what locks differs, and whether the value is a constant or computed."
2 · Constraints and numbers "The limits are lock time and replica lag. No statement may hold a blocking lock for more than a moment, and the backfill must not push replicas behind."
3 · Baseline design "So I expand, backfill, then contract. Add the column as nullable, which is a metadata change. Deploy code that writes it on every insert and update. Backfill old rows in small batches. Add the constraint last."
4 · Deep-dive "The backfill walks the primary key in small batches, one short transaction each, and pauses when replica lag rises. On PostgreSQL I add a check constraint as not valid, then validate it, which scans without blocking writes."
5 · Failure modes "The dangerous one is the lock queue. A schema change waiting behind a long transaction blocks every query behind it, so I set a lock timeout and retry."
6 · Evolve "Then it becomes a rule: every migration is expand and contract, checked in the pipeline."
Close "No step holds a long lock, and every step before the constraint can be undone."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
"Three answers change the plan."

Question Why it matters
Which engine and version? adding a column with a default is a metadata change on PostgreSQL 11+ and on MySQL 8.0 InnoDB (ALGORITHM=INSTANT); older versions rewrite the table
Is the value a constant or computed? a constant can be a default; a computed value needs a backfill
Do old application versions still write to the table? until they are gone, a NOT NULL constraint rejects their inserts
Are there replicas or CDC consumers? every backfilled row is replicated and emitted

Engine behaviour as generally documented; I'd confirm against the version in use.

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
"Two budgets, and the arithmetic of the backfill."

Budget Limit
Blocking lock on the table well under a second per statement
Replica lag stays inside the alert threshold throughout
Transaction size small enough that undo, the log and vacuum keep up 
rows              = 1,000,000,000            ← illustrative for a 500 GB table
batch             = 5,000 rows
batches           = 1,000,000,000 / 5,000    = 200,000
time per batch    = 0.2 s work + 0.3 s pause = 0.5 s
total             = 200,000 × 0.5 s          = 100,000 s ≈ 28 hours

So the backfill is a job that runs for a day or more, and must be resumable.

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
"Five steps; each one is short or non-blocking."

Step Lock Undo
1 · Add nullable brief exclusive, metadata only drop the column
2 · Deploy writers none roll the deploy back
3 · Backfill row locks, a batch at a time stop the job
4 · Validate allows reads and writes (PostgreSQL) drop the constraint
5 · Enforce brief point of no return for old application versions

Step 2 comes before step 3. Otherwise rows inserted during the backfill arrive empty and the job never finishes.

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.html:
"Walk the primary key; commit per batch." Run on SQLite through Python.

import sqlite3
m = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
m.execute("CREATE TABLE accounts(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT)")
m.executemany("INSERT INTO accounts(email) VALUES (?)",
              [(f"u{i}@x.com",) for i in range(1, 11)])
m.execute("ALTER TABLE accounts ADD COLUMN email_domain TEXT")  # expand
last = batches = 0
while True:
    ids = [r[0] for r in m.execute(
        "SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id > ? ORDER BY id LIMIT 4", (last,))]
    if not ids: break
    m.execute("UPDATE accounts SET email_domain = substr(email, "
              "instr(email, '@') + 1) WHERE id BETWEEN ? AND ?",
              (ids[0], ids[-1]))
    m.commit(); last = ids[-1]; batches += 1   # one short transaction
left = m.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM accounts "
                 "WHERE email_domain IS NULL").fetchone()[0]
print(batches, "batches;", left, "rows left NULL")
# → 3 batches; 0 rows left NULL
Property How
Resumable the last id is saved; a restart continues from it
Throttled pause while replica lag or lock waits are above the limit
Idempotent re-running a batch sets the same values
No OFFSET the key range is seeked, so batch 200,000 costs the same as batch 1
The constraint, on PostgreSQL 12+:ADD CONSTRAINT … CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALIDVALIDATE CONSTRAINTSET NOT NULL (uses the validated check, so no second scan)drop the check

On MySQL: an online schema-change tool (gh-ost, pt-online-schema-change) copies to a shadow table and swaps it in.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.claim: the lock queue and the long transaction
stages.html:
"What turns a metadata change into an outage."

Failure Cause Guard
Every query on the table stalls the ALTER waits behind a long transaction, and everything queues behind the ALTER lock_timeout of a second or two, then retry
Replicas fall behind the backfill writes faster than they apply throttle on lag
The log or undo space fills one huge transaction commit per batch
Inserts fail after step 5 an old application version doesn't set the column confirm no old writers; a default as a safety net
CDC consumers are flooded a billion update events tell the owners; filter or pause

Measure during the run: lock waits, replica lag, rows left NULL, write latency on the table.

stages.name: Evolve
stages.claim: make it the only way to migrate
stages.html:
"The pattern outlives this one change."

Practice Detail
Expand and contract for every change renames, type changes and splits follow the same steps
A migration linter in CI rejects a blocking ALTER, a missing lock timeout, an unbatched UPDATE
Schema and code deploy separately the schema is always compatible with the previous and the next application version
A backfill framework resumable, throttled, observable; not a one-off script each time

Fix layer: migration process, enforced in the pipeline.

followUps.question: "Just run ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN … NOT NULL DEFAULT 'x'."
followUps.html:
Safe only for a constant default on an engine that stores it as metadata.

Case Result
Constant default, PostgreSQL 11+ / MySQL 8.0 instant fast; still needs a lock timeout
Computed value, or an older version a full table rewrite under a blocking lock

followUps.question: 🧪 The backfill uses . What happens by batch 100,000?
followUps.html:
Each batch reads and throws away every row before it.

batch 100,000: OFFSET = 100,000 × 5,000 = 500,000,000 rows skipped   ← to update 5,000
keyset:        WHERE id > last ORDER BY id LIMIT 5000                ← seeks straight there

followUps.question: Why add the constraint as NOT VALID first?
followUps.html:
It splits a long blocking step into a short one and a non-blocking one.

  • NOT VALID: enforced for new writes at once; no scan.
  • VALIDATE: scans existing rows while reads and writes continue.

followUps.question: How do you roll back?
followUps.html:
Every step before enforcement has a one-line undo.

Undo:stop the backfilldrop the constraintroll back the writersdrop the column

After SET NOT NULL, rolling the application back to a version that doesn't write the column fails.

followUps.question: How do you stop the next engineer from running the blocking version?
followUps.html:
The pipeline refuses it.

Guard Catches
A migration linter blocking statements, missing timeouts
A default lock timeout for the migration role a queue building behind a waiting ALTER
Migrations tested on a production-sized copy a rewrite that takes hours

dontSay: "I'd run the ALTER at night." — a blocking lock at 3 a.m. is still an outage.
"One UPDATE to fill it in." — one transaction over 500 GB.
"Adding a column is instant." — on which engine, with which default?
"We'll take a short maintenance window." — the question said zero downtime.

databases-q48.testing: that you choose the key from the queries, check for skew, and have a plan for the tenant that outgrows a shard.
databases-q48.trap: sharding on an auto-increment id or a timestamp, or sharding before a single node is exhausted.
databases-q48.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "First I ask whether we need to shard yet. Indexes, replicas, partitioning and a bigger node come first. Then I ask for the queries, because the key is chosen from them."
2 · Constraints and numbers "A good key does three things: most queries touch one shard, load spreads evenly, and the key never changes for a row. I'd want the tenant size distribution, because one giant tenant changes the answer."
3 · Baseline design "In a multi-tenant product nearly every query is scoped to a tenant, so tenant id is the key. Every table carries it, and a tenant's joins and transactions stay on one shard."
4 · Deep-dive "The weakness is skew. So I don't hash tenants straight to shards. I use a directory that maps each tenant to a shard, which lets me give a large tenant its own shard and move tenants without rehashing everyone."
5 · Failure modes "What still hurts: cross-tenant reports, which fan out to every shard; globally unique ids; and a tenant too big for one node, which needs a second-level key inside it."
6 · Evolve "I'd watch load per shard and per tenant, and rebalance by moving tenants online."
Close "Tenant id through a directory: local queries, and a way out for the outliers."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: do we need shards, and what are the queries
stages.html:
"Sharding is the last step, so I check the earlier ones."

Before sharding:indexes and query fixesread replicascachingpartitioninga larger node ─measured write or size limitshard
Access pattern Scope Needs a transaction?
A tenant's users, projects, invoices one tenant yes, within the tenant
A tenant's dashboard joins one tenant no
Login by email global no
Admin report across all tenants all tenants no

Three of four are scoped to one tenant. That decides the key.

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
"Each candidate against the three tests."

Candidate key Queries stay on one shard Load is even Never changes
tenant_id yes, for tenant-scoped work only if tenants are similar in size yes
Row id (hash) no: a tenant is spread over every shard yes yes
Auto-increment id (range) no no: all new writes hit the last shard yes
created_at (range) no no: "now" is one hot shard yes
region partly no: a few values can change

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
"The key is in every table and every query."

projects(tenant_id, id, name, …)   PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, id)
invoices(tenant_id, id, …)         PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, id)
Design rule Reason
tenant_id leads every primary key and index routing and seeking use the same prefix
Every query carries tenant_id the router sends it to one shard
Joins and transactions stay inside a tenant they stay on one shard
Small global tables (plans, countries) copied to every shard as reference tables
Login by email a small global lookup: email → tenant

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.claim: skew, and the directory that absorbs it
stages.html:
"One large tenant makes one hot shard." Simulation: 39 tenants of 100 rows and one of 6,000, hashed to 4 shards.

import hashlib
def shard(key, n=4):
    return int(hashlib.md5(str(key).encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % n
tenants = {f"t{i}": 100 for i in range(1, 40)}
tenants["big"] = 6000                       # one giant tenant
by_tenant, by_row = [0] * 4, [0] * 4
for t, rows in tenants.items():
    by_tenant[shard(t)] += rows
    for r in range(rows):
        by_row[shard(f"{t}:{r}")] += 1
print(by_tenant)
print(by_row)
# → [6900, 1100, 1100, 800]
# → [2434, 2490, 2513, 2463]

Hashing by row is even and useless: every tenant query now hits all four shards.

The fix keeps the key and changes the mapping:

Mapping Placement Moving a tenant
hash(tenant_id) % N fixed by arithmetic changing N remaps almost everyone
A directory: tenant_id → shard chosen per tenant; the giant gets its own shard copy the tenant, flip one directory row

The directory is small, read on every request and rarely written, so it is cached and replicated.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
"Each loss needs an answer before launch."

Loss Answer
Cross-tenant queries fan out and merge, or run them on a warehouse fed by CDC
Cross-shard transactions designed out; where unavoidable, a saga
Global uniqueness (email, ids) a global lookup table; ids that embed the shard or are UUIDs
A tenant too large for one node a second-level key inside that tenant (tenant_id, project_id)
The directory is down cached in the router; it is the most available component
Schema changes run on every shard; versions must tolerate being mixed

Measure: rows, queries per second and storage per shard and per tenant; the share of queries that touch more than one shard.

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
"Growth is handled by moving entries in the directory."

Move a tenant:copy to the new shardreplicate changes until caught upbrief write pause for that tenantflip the directory rowdelete the old copy
Stage Change
Today tenants packed onto a few shards by the directory
A tenant grows moved to its own shard, online
Regulation the directory also places a tenant in a region
Many small tenants packed densely; noisy ones are rate-limited per tenant

Fix layer: data model (the key on every table) and routing (the directory).

followUps.question: "Shard on the primary key so load is perfectly even."
followUps.html:
Even load, and every useful query becomes a scatter.

Key One tenant's dashboard
Row id asks every shard, merges the results
tenant_id asks one shard

followUps.question: 🧪 Four shards by ; you add a fifth. Roughly what share of tenants move?
followUps.html:
About four in five.

a tenant stays only if  h % 4 == h % 5
that holds for 4 residues out of every 20   ← h % 20 in {0, 1, 2, 3}
stay = 4 / 20 = 20%      move = 80%

Consistent hashing or a directory moves only what has to move.

followUps.question: How do you run a report across all tenants?
followUps.html:
Not on the shards.

  • Occasional: fan out to every shard and merge.
  • Regular: a warehouse fed by CDC from all shards.

followUps.question: How do you generate unique ids across shards?
followUps.html:
Ids that can't collide by construction.

Scheme Note
(tenant_id, local id) composite key simplest; unique within the tenant
A time-ordered id with a shard or node part sortable, no coordination
Random UUID unique; poor index locality

followUps.question: When would you choose a database per tenant?
followUps.html:
When isolation matters more than operating cost.

Model Pick when
Shared tables, tenant_id column many small tenants; lowest cost
A schema or database per tenant strict isolation, per-tenant backup and restore, few large tenants
A mix through the directory most products: small tenants shared, large ones dedicated

dontSay: "We'll shard" as the first fix for a slow database. — replicas and partitioning first.
"Hash the primary key." — every tenant query fans out.
"Shard by date." — today is one hot shard.
"Tenants are about the same size." — measure the distribution.

databases-q49.testing: that you name the dual-write problem, reach for the transactional outbox, and say that consumers must be idempotent.
databases-q49.trap: "commit, then publish" (or the reverse) with a retry, as if that made it atomic.
databases-q49.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "This is the dual-write problem. A database commit and a broker publish are two systems, so they can't be one atomic step. First I ask what's worse here: a lost event, or a duplicate."
2 · Constraints and numbers "Usually a lost event is unacceptable and a duplicate is tolerable. So I want at-least-once delivery, and a bound on how late an event may be."
3 · Baseline design "I use a transactional outbox. In the same local transaction that inserts the order, I insert a row into an outbox table. Both commit or neither does."
4 · Deep-dive "A relay then reads the outbox and publishes: a poller, or change data capture on the log. It marks a row as sent only after the broker acknowledges."
5 · Failure modes "If the relay crashes after publishing and before marking, the event goes out twice. So every event carries an id, and the consumer records ids it has processed and skips repeats."
6 · Evolve "For a flow across several services I chain these into a saga, with a compensating action per step."
Close "One local transaction, at-least-once delivery, idempotent consumers."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
"Either order of two writes has a gap."

Order Crash in the gap Result
Commit, then publish after the commit an order exists and nobody is told
Publish, then commit after the publish an event announces an order that doesn't exist
Publish inside the transaction the commit fails after the publish the same phantom event

A retry narrows the gap. It doesn't close it: the process can die before it retries.

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
"Three delivery guarantees; one is practical."

Guarantee Meaning Cost
At-most-once may lose an event none; unacceptable for orders
At-least-once never loses; may repeat consumers must be idempotent
Exactly-once effect at-least-once delivery + an idempotent consumer a processed-ids record
Number to agree Why
Maximum delay from commit to publish sets the polling interval or justifies CDC
Ordering needed? per order, or global decides the partition key
How long consumers remember ids bounds the dedupe table

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.claim: the outbox row in the same transaction
stages.html:
"The event becomes data in my own database first."

outbox(id, aggregate_id, topic, payload, created_at, sent_at)

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.claim: atomic write, duplicate delivery, one effect
stages.html:
"A crash before commit leaves nothing; a duplicate is absorbed." Run on SQLite through Python.

import sqlite3
o = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
o.executescript("CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, total INT);"
                "CREATE TABLE outbox(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, payload TEXT,"
                " sent INT DEFAULT 0);")
def place_order(total, crash=False):
    try:
        with o:                                # one local transaction
            oid = o.execute("INSERT INTO orders(total) VALUES (?)",
                            (total,)).lastrowid
            o.execute("INSERT INTO outbox(payload) VALUES (?)", (str(oid),))
            if crash: raise RuntimeError("crash before commit")
    except RuntimeError: pass
place_order(50); place_order(70, crash=True)
print(o.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders").fetchone()[0], "orders,",
      o.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM outbox").fetchone()[0], "outbox rows")
seen, delivered = set(), []
for mid, payload in o.execute("SELECT id, payload FROM outbox").fetchall():
    for _ in range(2):                         # the relay publishes twice
        if mid not in seen: seen.add(mid); delivered.append(payload)
print("delivered:", delivered)
# → 1 orders, 1 outbox rows
# → delivered: ['1']
Relay style How Pick when
Polling select unsent rows every interval; mark sent after the ack simple; a delay of the interval is fine
CDC on the log a log reader streams outbox inserts to the broker low delay; no polling load

Ordering: publish with the aggregate id (the order id) as the partition key, so one order's events stay in order.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
"Every crash point ends in a retry or a duplicate, never a loss."

Crash point State left Outcome
Before the commit no order, no outbox row nothing happened
After the commit, before the publish an unsent row the relay publishes it later
After the publish, before "mark sent" still unsent published again → the consumer dedupes
The broker is down rows accumulate published when it returns; alert on backlog
The consumer fails mid-way no ack redelivered; its work and its "processed" record commit together
Also watch Guard
The outbox table grows delete or archive sent rows
A poison event blocks the queue a dead-letter queue after N attempts
Several relays SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, or a single leader

Measure: outbox backlog and the age of the oldest unsent row.

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
"One outbox per service, chained."

Saga:order placedpayment takenstock reservedcompensate: refund paymentcancel order
Option Atomic across systems? Why I do or don't
Outbox no: eventual, never lost the default
Saga no: each step is local, with a compensation multi-service business flows
Two-phase commit yes blocks if the coordinator fails; few brokers support it
Event sourcing the event log is the write when the events are the model, not a side effect

Fix layer: write path in the service; idempotency in every consumer.

followUps.question: "Publish after the commit, and retry on failure."
followUps.html:
The process can die between the commit and the publish, and the retry dies with it.

Gap:commit crashpublish never runsnothing records that an event is owed

The outbox row is that record.

followUps.question: 🧪 The relay publishes event 17, then crashes before marking it sent. What does the consumer see?
followUps.html:
Event 17 twice. Its effect is applied once.

relay restarts → row 17 still unsent → publishes 17 again
consumer: 17 already in processed_events → skip          ← at-least-once + idempotent

followUps.question: How does a consumer become idempotent?
followUps.html:
It makes "already done" a fact it can check.

Technique How
A processed-events table insert the event id in the same transaction as the work; a unique-key violation means skip
A naturally idempotent write "set status = paid", not "add 1"

followUps.question: Polling or CDC for the relay?
followUps.html:
Polling to start; CDC when delay or load matters.

  • Polling: nothing new to run; adds query load and a delay.
  • CDC: near-real-time and in commit order; one more system to operate.

followUps.question: Why not two-phase commit?
followUps.html:
It trades availability for atomicity, and most stacks can't run it.

Two-phase commit Outbox
If the coordinator fails participants hold locks and wait nothing is blocked
Broker support rare any broker
Consistency atomic eventual, with no loss

dontSay: "I'd wrap both in a transaction." — the broker isn't in the database's transaction.
"Commit, then publish, with retries." — the crash is between them.
"The broker gives exactly-once." — the effect is exactly-once only with an idempotent consumer.
"Duplicates won't happen." — they're the price of never losing an event.

databases-q55.testing: that the hard part is semantics, not syntax, and that safety includes "plausible wrong numbers", not just dropped tables.
databases-q55.trap: "the model generates SQL against our warehouse schema", read-write, with no semantic layer.
databases-q55.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I'd ask which metrics executives actually ask about, which warehouse, who owns the definitions, and what the data-access rules are."
2 · Constraints and numbers "The constraints are cost and trust. A bad join over a large fact table can scan a huge amount of data, so every query has a time limit and a scan limit. And a wrong number in a board deck is worse than an error."
3 · Baseline design "Generating valid SQL is the easy part. The hard part is meaning: what 'revenue' is here, which date defines 'last quarter', which of three customer tables is the real one. So the agent queries a curated semantic layer, with governed metric definitions and approved views, not raw tables. For common metrics it calls metric tools and writes no SQL at all."
4 · Deep-dive "Then verification. It shows the SQL and the definitions it used, checks results against known totals or the previous period, and when a question is ambiguous it asks, or states its assumption."
5 · Failure modes "The failures that matter are plausible wrong answers: a wrong definition, a join that double-counts, stale data. Safety is read-only credentials scoped to the user, row-level security in the database, and select statements only."
6 · Evolve "It grows by adding metrics and views where unanswered questions cluster, with a golden set of business questions checked by result."
Close "The risk isn't a dropped table; it's a confident number that's wrong."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: users, questions, data and its owners
stages.html:
"Four questions, and the third is the one teams skip."

Question Sets
Which metrics do executives ask about? the metric tools to build first
Which warehouse, how large? cost limits
Who owns each definition? the semantic layer's governance
What may each user see? row-level security

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
"Every query runs inside limits set before the model writes anything."

per-question budget (illustrative)
at most 3 model steps: understand, query, explain
per query: time-out 30 s · scan cap · row cap 10,000
answer in under about 10 s for a metric tool; longer for ad-hoc SQL, with progress shown
Limit Prevents
Time-out and scan cap a runaway query bill
Row cap a result too large for the context

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
"The agent's choices are narrowed to correct ones."

Path:questionambiguous? askmetric tool if one fitsSQL over approved viewslimits + read-onlysanity checkanswer with SQL and definitions
Control Setting Prevents
Credentials read-only role, user-scoped, row-level security writes; data leaks
Statements SELECT only, by a parser allow-list schema or data changes
Scope approved views and metric definitions wrong tables and definitions
Limits time-out, scan cap, row cap runaway cost
Output SQL + definitions + assumptions shown silent wrong numbers
Check compare with known totals or the prior period implausible results

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.html:
"A query that runs cleanly proves nothing about meaning."

Ambiguous term Possible readings What the agent does
"Revenue" gross, net of refunds, recognised uses the governed metric; names it
"Last quarter" calendar, fiscal; order date or invoice date asks, or states the assumption
"Customers" accounts, users, paying accounts asks, or states the assumption
Verify:resultcompare with a trusted dashboard totalflag, don't present

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
"None of these raises an error."

Failure Control
A wrong metric definition metric tools from the semantic layer
A fan-out join double-counts documented joins; sanity checks on totals
Stale data data freshness shown with the answer
Instructions hidden in data values read-only, no actions; results are treated as data
Different SQL on each run metric tools make the common answers deterministic

stages.name: Evolve
stages.claim: grow the semantic layer from questions
stages.html:
"Unanswered questions are the roadmap."

Loop:log unanswered or corrected questionscluster themadd metrics and viewsadd golden cases
Golden question Expected result Runs
"Net revenue last fiscal quarter" the governed total measure, several times
An ambiguous question a clarifying question or a stated assumption measure

Evaluation hook: golden business questions compared by result set, not by SQL text. Fix layer: retrieval/data (the semantic layer) and permission system.

followUps.question: Why not give it the whole schema?
followUps.html:
Hundreds of tables overwhelm the context and invite wrong joins.

Whole schema Curated layer
Many plausible, wrong choices fewer, correct ones
Definitions chosen by the model definitions governed by owners

followUps.question: "Read-only means it's safe."
followUps.html:
It stops damage to the data, and nothing else.

  • Not prevented: a wrong number in a board deck.
  • Not prevented: a full table scan with a large bill.

followUps.question: 🧪 Two runs give different revenue numbers for the same question. Why?
followUps.html:
Different SQL each time, so a different definition each time.

run 1: SUM(order_total)                    ← gross
run 2: SUM(order_total) − SUM(refunds)     ← net
fix: a governed "net_revenue" metric tool, so the definition isn't chosen per run

followUps.question: How do you evaluate it?
followUps.html:
Golden business questions with known results.

  • Compared by result set, not by SQL text.
  • Run several times for consistency.
  • Including ambiguous questions, where the right behaviour is to ask.

dontSay: "We give the model the schema and run whatever it writes." — no semantic layer, no limits.
Safety that's only about DROP TABLE. — the costly failure is a wrong number.
"The query ran, so the answer is right." — running isn't meaning.
